summary:
Our project involves developing an interactive website that allows users to identify, visualize, and compare locations on Earth that share topographical and geographical characteristics with Mars and the Moon. The platform aims to identify potential sites suitable for establishing future research bases and safe landing zones.
Using topographical data and visualization tools, the website allows users to explore different regions on Earth, analyze their terrain features, and recognize similarities with the surfaces of other celestial bodies.
This project is important because it helps improve the understanding and analysis of potential environments for future space missions. Furthermore, it provides a digital tool that can support scientific research, mission planning, and collaboration across different disciplines involved in space exploration.
details:
Another World at Home

What does it do or how does it work?
Our project identifies locations on Earth that share geological, thermal, chemical, and climatic characteristics with the Moon and Mars. These places are known as planetary analogs. Before sending rovers, instruments, or astronauts, space agencies need to test their technology in real, extreme environments. We researched and selected four groups of sites, and for each one we explain why it resembles the celestial body, what is tested there, and its exact coordinates:

  • Lunar analogs: the Kīlauea and Mauna Kea volcanoes (Hawaii, USA), whose basaltic lava, ash, and rugged terrain resemble the lunar maria. Also the lava tube field at Lava Beds (California, USA), which reproduces the underground caves found on the Moon, and the Askja volcano (Iceland), where black basalt and ash-covered ice mimic the lunar poles.
  • Martian analogs: the Atacama Desert (Chile), the driest and oldest non-polar desert on Earth, with high UV radiation and oxidized, salt-rich soils. Also Haughton Crater on Devon Island (Canadian Arctic), a cold, rocky polar desert with a 23 km impact crater.

What are its benefits?

  • It reduces risks and costs, because technology is tested on Earth before being sent into space.
  • It helps identify suitable sites for permanent research bases and safe landing zones.
  • It allows testing of rovers, handheld geological tools, navigation cameras, pressurized spacesuits, ground-penetrating radar, deep-drilling robots, life support systems, and crew isolation protocols.
  • It brings together scattered information in one place, useful for students, scientists, and space agencies.

What is the expected impact?
We hope to help prepare for future lunar and Martian operations, which require the expertise of many disciplines: geology, engineering, astrobiology, robotics, and space medicine. By showing that Earth offers accessible “other worlds,” we also aim to bring space exploration closer to the public and spark interest in science, especially among young people. These locations are ideal for NASA research and experiments because of their similarities to the Moon and Mars.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
Due to time constraints, we did not develop a web page, so we presented the project as a slide presentation. We used PowerPoint for the design and organized the information from NASA sources: Planetary Analog Explorer, Planetary Analogs, and Analog Missions. To locate each site, we used precise geographic coordinates, and we worked from personal computers. We did not use programming languages in this version.

How is your project creative?
It changes the usual perspective: instead of looking only toward space, it looks at our own planet to find “other worlds.” It connects real, well-known places with the challenges of living on the Moon and Mars, and it organizes the information clearly: each site is explained by why it is similar, what is tested there, and where it is located. The name, Another World at Home, sums up that idea.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific similarity: geology, temperature, humidity, radiation, soil composition, and terrain.
  • Practical usefulness: which technologies and protocols can be tested at each location.
  • Diversity: we included both lunar and Martian analogs, and different types of environments (volcanic, desert, polar, and underground).
  • Reliability: we used official NASA sources and verifiable coordinates.
  • Time and resources: given the time available, we chose a presentation instead of a web page, leaving it as a foundation to expand in the future.
